study.title: Romans 4 - Abraham, faith and imputed righteousness
study.overview: Romans 4 presents Abraham as a biblical proof that justification comes by faith and not by works, circumcision, nor by the Law. Paul also uses David to show that the bliss of forgiveness depends on God to attribute righteousness to the sinner, and not from human merit. The chapter ends by applying Abraham's example to those who believe in Jesus, whose death and resurrection ground our justification.

outline.title: Abraham was told righteous by faith
outline.explanation: Paul asks what Abraham obtained and answers with the Scripture: he believed in God, and this faith was told him as righteousness. Thus, the reward of justification is not wages due for works, but favor received by faith. David is quoted to reinforce that God forgives and does not take into account the sin of the one to whom he declares righteous.

outline.title: The faith of Abraham came before circumcision
outline.explanation: Paul shows that the righteousness attributed to Abraham happened when he was still uncircumcised. Circumcision came later as a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith, that Abraham might be the father of both uncicision believers and of Jews walking in the same footsteps of faith.

outline.title: The promise depends on faith and grace
outline.explanation: The inheritance promised to Abraham did not come by the Law, for this would nullify the promise and empty the faith. Instead, the promise is confirmed by grace and received by faith. Paul describes Abraham's faith as trust in the God who gives life to the dead and fulfills what he promises, even against every human appearance.

outline.title: Abraham points to those who believe in Jesus
outline.explanation: The account of Abraham was written not only to him, but also to us. The same righteousness will be imputed to those who believe in God, who raised up Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up because of our sins and rose again for our justification.

study.context: The notes highlight that, in Paul's time, many Jews honored Abraham as the founder of Israel and some Jewish texts presented him in order to support his dignity by works, obedience or circumcision. Paul responds to this reading by Scripture that Abraham's position before God came by faith. The chapter also dialogues with the Jewish reading of the Psalms and the Genesis account, and uses these texts to defend that justification by faith is central in God's plan.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that justification is the act of God, not human conquest. Faith is not a meritorious work; it is the means by which a person fully leans on divine mercy. Therefore, the wages of works is not the model of salvation: when God justifies the ungodly, he attributes justice to the believing sinner without treating his acceptance as debt. Circumcision, in turn, is a later sign, no cause of justification. The promise given to Abraham also reveals that grace reaches Jews and Gentiles. Paul anchors everything in God's ability to give life to the dead, which prepares the Christological reading of the end of the chapter: the resurrection of Jesus confirms that the atoning work of Christ was accepted by God and that the justification of believers is safe. Thus, Abraham's faith and Christian faith have the same foundation: to trust in the God who fulfills his word when everything seems impossible.

scholarViews.insight: Paul teaches that faith, and not obedience, established Abraham's position before God; this justification by faith is central in the divine plan.
Abraham's faith was counted as righteousness before circumcision, which shows that bliss belongs not only to the circumcised, but also to the uncircumcised.
The promise to Abraham did not come by the Law, therefore, if the heirs came through it, faith would lose its function and the promise would be void.

questions: What in my religious practice could I be treating as merit, when the chapter insists that everything depends on the grace received by faith?
Is my trust in the God who gives life to the dead, or in the human evidence that something is already resolved?
How does Abraham's faith correct my way of seeing signs, tradition and religious belonging?
study.practice: Take this chapter to prayer by asking God to start you all trust in self merit. Confess that acceptance before God comes by Christ and not for religious performance. At the same time, imitate Abraham: believe in God's promise even when the situation seems dead, and acts with obedience as a fruit of this faith, not as an attempt to buy it.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not bring extensive historical data nor allow to affirm details beyond what they mention about the Jewish reception of Abraham and Paul's argumentation. There is also no basis here for developing specific confessional debates on circumcision or alliance beyond the textual meaning presented. Some commentators emphasize different aspects, but all converge on justification by faith as the central theme of the chapter.
